key_terms.meaning: A document vector whose j-th entry is the count of vocabulary word j in that document; word order is discarded.
How many times a term t occurs in document d; often stored as tf(t,d) or as tf(t,d) ÷ (total terms in d).
idf(t) = log(N ÷ df(t)), where N is the number of documents and df(t) is how many documents contain t; rare words get large weight.
w(t,d) = tf(t,d) × idf(t); a term scores high when it is frequent in this document but rare across the collection.
Picks the label c that maximises P(c) × Π P(wᵢ | c), assuming words are independent given the class.
A linear model that computes P(y=1 | x) = σ(w·x + b), with σ the sigmoid; weights are learned by minimising log loss.
Finds the separating hyperplane with the largest margin; the soft-margin form uses slack variables and a C parameter to allow errors.
Replaces P(w|c) = count(w,c) ÷ count(c) by (count(w,c)+1) ÷ (count(c)+|V|) so unseen words do not get probability zero.
Precision = TP ÷ (TP+FP), recall = TP ÷ (TP+FN), F1 = 2PR ÷ (P+R); all computed per class from a confusion matrix.
A table of predicted label against true label; its diagonal holds correct decisions and the rest hold error types.
Macro-F1 averages F1 over classes without weighting; micro-F1 pools all decisions first, so it is dominated by frequent classes.
Sum or average pre-assigned polarity scores of the words in a text, with rules for negation and intensifiers, to get a polarity score.
Predicts a polarity for each mentioned aspect of an entity, for example battery and camera in a phone review, not one polarity for the whole text.
A vector of length |V| with 1 at the index of the word and 0 elsewhere; every pair of distinct words has cosine similarity 0.
cos(u,v) = (u·v) ÷ (‖u‖ ‖v‖); it compares direction only, so it ignores document length.
A shallow neural model trained to predict context words from a word (skip-gram) or a word from its context (CBOW), giving dense vectors of 50–300 dimensions.
Builds vectors by factorising a global word–word co-occurrence matrix so that wᵢ·w̃ⱼ + bᵢ + b̃ⱼ ≈ log co-occurrence count.
Extends Word2Vec with a document vector trained jointly with word vectors, so each whole document gets one dense vector.
Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings; this is the assumption behind all count-based and neural embeddings.
Groups document vectors into k clusters by repeating assignment to the nearest centroid and recomputation of centroids until they stop moving.

takeaways: A document becomes a fixed-length numeric vector through bag of words or TF-IDF, and everything downstream depends on that vector.
TF-IDF down-weights words that appear in most documents, so common words like 'the' stop dominating the feature vector.
Naive Bayes is fast and works with tiny training sets; logistic regression and SVM usually win when labelled data is plentiful.
Accuracy lies on skewed classes; precision, recall and macro-F1 on a confusion matrix show the real behaviour.
Lexicon methods need no training data but fail on sarcasm and domain words; trained classifiers need labelled examples but adapt to the domain.
A one-hot vector carries no notion of similarity, while a dense embedding places similar words close together in space.
Word2Vec learns from local context windows, GloVe from global co-occurrence counts; both end up with vectors where cosine similarity approximates relatedness.
Distributional similarity gives both word vectors and document vectors, and document vectors can be clustered without any labels.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from feature construction (BoW, TF-IDF weights written out) through the classifier's objective and decision rule, and to finish with the evaluation metric that would actually decide the choice.

bank.q: Explain how a raw text document is converted into a TF-IDF vector. Write the formulas for term frequency and inverse document frequency, and explain why the product is used instead of raw counts.
outline: Vocabulary is built from the training corpus after tokenisation and normalisation
tf(t,d) counts the term or divides by document length; idf(t) = log(N ÷ df(t))
Product w(t,d) = tf × idf gives high weight to terms frequent here and rare elsewhere
Common stopwords get idf near zero, so their contribution shrinks
Result is a sparse vector of length |V|, one per document, ready for a classifier

bank.q: State the Naive Bayes assumption for text classification and derive the decision rule from Bayes' theorem. Show how Laplace smoothing changes the estimate.
outline: Bayes: P(c|d) ∝ P(c) Π P(wᵢ|c)
Conditional independence of words given the class is the 'naive' part
Estimate P(c) from class frequencies; P(wᵢ|c) from counts within the class
Unseen word gives zero, so add-one smoothing with |V| in the denominator
Predict the class with the maximum posterior; work in log space to avoid underflow

bank.q: Define precision, recall and F1 for a two-class text classifier and explain, with a spam-filter example, why accuracy alone can mislead.
outline: Definitions in terms of TP, FP, FN, TN
F1 as the harmonic mean, and why harmonic rather than arithmetic mean
Example where 95 percent of documents are 'not spam', so a constant classifier gets 95 percent accuracy
Precision and recall of that constant classifier are zero or undefined
Conclusion: report per-class metrics or macro-F1

bank.q: Compare one-hot word vectors with dense word embeddings in terms of dimensionality, sparsity, and ability to express similarity.
outline: One-hot has length |V|, is sparse, has exactly one 1
All distinct one-hot vectors are orthogonal, so cosine similarity is 0
Dense embeddings have 50–300 dimensions, all entries real numbers
Similar words get high cosine similarity by construction of training
Trade-off: one-hot is exact and interpretation-free, embeddings generalise

bank.q: A training set has 1000 documents, of which 200 are 'positive'. The word 'excellent' appears in 60 positive and 10 negative documents. With add-one smoothing over a vocabulary of 5000 words, compute the smoothed likelihoods and state which class the word favours.
outline: P(excellent|pos) = (60+1) ÷ (total positive word tokens + 5000)
P(excellent|neg) = (10+1) ÷ (total negative word tokens + 5000)
Prior P(pos) = 0.2, P(neg) = 0.8
Likelihood ratio is about 6, prior ratio is about 0.25, so combine both
Show the log-space arithmetic and the final comparison

bank.q: Describe how you would build a sentiment classifier for product reviews on an e-commerce site. Cover label definition, features beyond unigrams, class imbalance, and the metric you would report.
outline: Define labels from star ratings, e.g. 1–2 negative, 4–5 positive, drop the middle
Features: unigrams and bigrams, negation handling, TF-IDF weighting, review length
Handle class imbalance with class weights or resampling
Report macro-F1 and the confusion matrix, not plain accuracy
Validate on held-out reviews from the same product category

bank.q: Explain the skip-gram Word2Vec training procedure. Write the objective it maximises and explain how negative sampling makes it practical for a large vocabulary.
outline: Slide a context window of size m over the corpus
Objective: maximise Σ Σ log P(w_{t+j} | w_t) over context words
Softmax over the full vocabulary is expensive: O(|V|) per update
Negative sampling replaces it with a binary task against k random words
Result: dense vectors where the dot product of a word and its context is large

bank.q: You have 20,000 unlabelled news articles. Describe how to represent them and cluster them, including choice of vector, distance measure, choice of k, and how you would judge the clusters.
outline: TF-IDF vectors or averaged Doc2Vec vectors
Cosine distance is preferred over Euclidean for text
k-means with several random starts; pick k by silhouette score or elbow
Inspect top terms per cluster, not just the numeric score
Limitation: cluster labels are uninterpretable without human reading

bank.q: Show how a linear SVM classifies a TF-IDF document vector. Write the decision function, explain the margin, and say what the C parameter controls.
outline: Decision: f(x) = sign(w·x + b)
Margin is 2 ÷ ‖w‖; maximise it subject to correct classification
Soft margin adds slack variables ξᵢ with penalty C Σ ξᵢ
Small C means a wide, tolerant margin; large C means few training errors
Sparse TF-IDF vectors make the dot product cheap

bank.q: Compare lexicon-based and machine-learning sentiment analysis. For each, state the resource needed, the failure modes, and the situation where it would be the better choice.
outline: Lexicon: needs a polarity word list and negation rules; no training data
Lexicon fails on sarcasm, domain-specific words, and context-dependent polarity
ML: needs labelled data; learns domain words and combinations automatically
ML fails when the test domain differs from training domain
Recommendation: lexicon for a quick baseline or a new domain with no labels; ML when labelled data exists and accuracy matters

bank.q: A team reports 96 percent accuracy on a fake-news classifier where 4 percent of articles are fake. Analyse the result, state what additional numbers you need, and propose a better evaluation plan.
outline: Accuracy is inflated by the majority class; a constant 'real' predictor already gets 96 percent
Ask for the confusion matrix, per-class precision and recall
Macro-F1 and the false-negative rate on the fake class matter most
Consider precision at a fixed recall if editorial review capacity is limited
Recommend stratified splits and a held-out set from a later time period

bank.q: Word vectors trained on one corpus are used for document clustering of another corpus. Evaluate the risks and describe how you would check whether the representation is suitable.
outline: Domain and time shift change word usage, so neighbours may be wrong
Rare and out-of-vocabulary words get poor vectors
Check intrinsic quality on similarity benchmarks and by inspecting nearest neighbours
Check extrinsic quality: cluster purity on a small hand-labelled sample
Alternatives: train in-domain embeddings, use FastText subwords, or fall back to TF-IDF

bank.q: Discuss whether a bag-of-words representation can ever be enough for text classification. Support your answer with cases where word order matters and with the practical costs of richer representations.
outline: Bag of words discards order, so 'dog bites man' equals 'man bites dog'
Topic classification and spam filtering work well with n-grams and TF-IDF
Negation, sarcasm and aspect sentiment need order or syntax
Richer models cost more data, more compute and lose interpretability
Practical rule: start sparse, move to embeddings when data justifies it

glossary.def: Splitting a string of characters into words, punctuation marks or subword pieces.
A very frequent word such as 'the' or 'is' that is often removed or down-weighted because it carries little topical signal.
Crudely cutting a word to a common root, so 'running' and 'runs' both become 'run'.
Reducing a word to its dictionary form using grammatical knowledge, so 'better' becomes 'good'.
The set of distinct terms kept after preprocessing; its size is written |V|.
A vector with mostly zero entries, as produced by bag of words and TF-IDF.
The number of documents in the collection that contain a given term.
σ(z) = 1 ÷ (1 + e⁻ᶻ), which maps any real number to a probability between 0 and 1.
The negative log probability the model assigns to the correct label; minimising it trains logistic regression.
The set of points satisfying w·x + b = 0; in text classification it is the decision boundary between classes.
The distance between the separating hyperplane and the nearest training points; SVM maximises it.
Computing dot products in a higher-dimensional space without explicitly mapping the data there.
A training set where one label is far more frequent than another, which biases accuracy as a metric.
Averaging a metric over classes with equal weight for each class, regardless of class size.
The positive, negative or neutral orientation assigned to a word, phrase or document in sentiment analysis.
A rule that flips or reduces the polarity of words appearing after 'not', 'never' or 'no' within a short scope.
A dense, low-dimensional learned vector that represents a word, sentence or document.
The number of words to the left and right of a target word that a Word2Vec model treats as its context.
A training shortcut that teaches the model to separate real context words from a few randomly drawn fake ones.
A table whose entry (i,j) counts how often word j appears near word i in a corpus.
A word in the test data that never appeared in training, so no learned vector exists for it.
A clustering quality measure comparing how close a point is to its own cluster against the nearest other cluster.
The mean vector of all points currently assigned to a cluster.
The task of finding and labelling names of people, places, organisations and similar categories in text.
